Baseline Synchrony Calculation

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

Purpose

This file runs the actual synchrony analysis that the Baseline Synchrony Processing pipeline works up to. It takes the long-format positive- and negative-valence baseline warmth data produced by that pipeline and asks, second by second, whether mom’s and partner’s warmth track each other during the interaction, and whether one partner’s warmth tends to change before the other’s.

For each couple and each valence (positive, negative), the file fits an ARIMA model to each partner’s warmth time series and uses the residuals (the pre-whitened series) to compute a time-lagged cross-correlation function (CCF) between mom and partner. A bootstrap null distribution, built by independently reshuffling each partner’s residuals, establishes which lags show correlation stronger than chance. From that CCF, the file extracts several couple-level synchrony summaries: the single strongest lag overall, the strongest lag restricted to non-zero (time-lagged) lags, concurrent (lag-zero) synchrony, and how long it takes each couple to reach their first significant lag.

Throughout, a positive lag means partner’s warmth at the current second correlates with mom’s warmth a few seconds later, so partner is leading and mom is following. A negative lag means the reverse: mom’s warmth precedes partner’s, so mom is leading. This direction follows directly from how R’s ccf() function is called below (ccf(mom, partner)), and it is applied consistently to every leader/lag interpretation in this file.

The positive and negative sections mirror each other almost exactly, so the narrative under the negative section is kept brief where the logic has already been explained above.

Long-format positive- and negative-valence baseline warmth data, produced by the Baseline Synchrony Processing pipeline, are read in from where that processed data already lives.

Positive Interaction

This section calculates synchrony for positive warmth: how closely mom’s and partner’s warm, affectionate behavior track each other, and which partner’s warmth tends to lead the other’s during positive moments of the interaction.

Synchrony Calculation

The function below does the full per-couple synchrony calculation in three steps. First, it pre-whitens each partner’s warmth series with auto.arima() so the cross-correlation reflects genuine coupling between partners rather than each person’s own autocorrelation over time. Second, it computes the observed cross-correlation function between mom’s and partner’s residuals across a range of lags. Third, it builds a bootstrap null distribution by independently reshuffling each partner’s residuals, then flags any lag where the observed correlation falls outside the resulting 95% interval as significant.

ccf(mom, partner) at lag k estimates the correlation between mom’s residual at time t + k and partner’s residual at time t. A positive k means mom’s future value resembles partner’s current value, so partner is leading. A negative k means mom’s earlier value resembles partner’s current value, so mom is leading.

code 
# Function to compute time-lagged cross-correlation synchrony between dyad members
compute_blpwh_sync <- function(df, lag = 20, n_boot = 1000) {
  
  # Remove rows with missing data for both mom and partner variables
  df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(blmpwh), !is.na(blfpwh))
  
  # Check if there's enough data to compute lagged correlations
  if (nrow(df) < lag + 1) return(
    tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 1: Pre-whitening via ARIMA to remove autocorrelation ---
  # Fit models to each person's time series to account for individual patterns
  fit_mom <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blmpwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  fit_partner <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blfpwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  
  # If either model fails, return NA results
  if (is.null(fit_mom) || is.null(fit_partner)) return(
    tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # Extract residuals (pre-whitened series) - these represent deviations from                                                     each person's own temporal pattern
  res_mom <- residuals(fit_mom)
  res_partner <- residuals(fit_partner)
  
  # Combine residuals and remove any remaining missing values
  residuals_df <- tibble(res_mom, res_partner) %>% drop_na()
  if (nrow(residuals_df) < lag + 1) return(
    tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 2: Compute observed cross-correlation function (CCF) ---
  # ccf(mom, partner)[k] estimates cor(mom[t+k], partner[t]).
  # Negative lags: 
  ### mom's earlier value resembles partner's current value -> mom leads partner.
  # Positive lags: 
  ### mom's future value resembles partner's current value -> partner leads mom.
  ccf_result <- ccf(
    residuals_df$res_mom, residuals_df$res_partner, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)
  observed_acf <- ccf_result$acf  # Cross-correlation values at each lag
  lags <- ccf_result$lag           # Lag values (e.g., -20 to +20)
  
  # --- STEP 3: Bootstrap to establish confidence intervals ---
  # Create matrix to store bootstrap results
  boot_corrs <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = length(lags))
  n <- nrow(residuals_df)
  
  # Generate null distribution by randomly shuffling residuals 
  ### breaks temporal coupling
  for (i in 1:n_boot) {
    # Resample mom's residuals
    x_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_mom, n, replace = TRUE)    
    # Resample partner's residuals
    y_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_partner, n, replace = TRUE)  
    # Compute CCF on shuffled data
    boot_ccf <- ccf(x_boot, y_boot, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)   
    # Store correlation values
    boot_corrs[i, ] <- boot_ccf$acf 
  }
  
  # Calculate 95% confidence intervals from bootstrap distribution
  lower_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
  upper_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Determine significance: observed correlation falls outside 95% CI
  significant <- (observed_acf < lower_ci) | (observed_acf > upper_ci)
  
  # Return tibble with lag values, correlations, CIs, and significance
  tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(lags),
    acf = as.numeric(observed_acf),
    lower_ci = lower_ci,
    upper_ci = upper_ci,
    significant = significant
  )
}

The function above runs once per couple. The chunk below nests the long-format data by couple ID, applies the function to each couple’s data in turn, and unnests the results back into one row per couple per lag.

code 
# Nest data by couple ID (creates list-column with each dyad's time series)
blpwh_sync_id <- BL_WH_Long %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  nest()

# Apply the synchrony function to each couple's data
blpwh_sync_id <- blpwh_sync_id %>%
  mutate(blpwh_sync_ccf = map(data, compute_blpwh_sync))

# Unnest results to get one row per couple per lag value
blpwh_sync_results <- unnest(blpwh_sync_id, blpwh_sync_ccf)

blpwh_sync_results$lag <- as.numeric(blpwh_sync_results$lag)

Max Synchrony

For each couple, this pulls out the single lag with the strongest absolute correlation across the full range of lags (including lag zero), regardless of direction. This is the point of tightest overall coupling between mom’s and partner’s positive warmth.

code 
# Extract max synchrony for each couple
blpwh_sync_max <- blpwh_sync_results %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  # Find the row with maximum absolute correlation for each couple
  slice_max(abs(acf), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  select(ID, 
         max_lag = lag,           # Lag at which max occurs
         max_sync = acf,          # Correlation value (with sign)
         max_abs_sync = acf,      # Will convert to absolute
         lower_ci, 
         upper_ci, 
         significant) %>%
  mutate(max_abs_sync = abs(max_sync)) %>%  # Add absolute value column
  ungroup()

Max Synchrony Interpretation

This translates the raw max-synchrony lag into a plain-language leader label, using the direction established above (negative lag, mom leads; positive lag, partner leads), and adds a rough strength category based on the size of the correlation.

code 
# Add interpretation columns
blpwh_sync_max_interpret <- blpwh_sync_max %>%
  mutate(
    # Who leads? Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads
    leader = case_when(
      max_lag < 0 ~ "Mom leads",
      max_lag > 0 ~ "Partner leads",
      max_lag == 0 ~ "Concurrent",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    # How much lead time?
    lead_time_seconds = abs(max_lag),
    # Direction of relationship
    relationship = case_when(
      max_sync > 0 ~ "Positive (same direction)",
      max_sync < 0 ~ "Negative (opposite direction)",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    # Strength categorization (example thresholds)
    strength = case_when(
      max_abs_sync >= 0.5 ~ "Strong",
      max_abs_sync >= 0.3 ~ "Moderate",
      max_abs_sync >= 0.1 ~ "Weak",
      TRUE ~ "Very weak"
    )
  )

blpwh_sync_max_interpret_preview <- blpwh_sync_max_interpret %>%
  select(ID, max_sync, max_lag, leader, lead_time_seconds,
         relationship, strength, significant)

knitr::kable(head(blpwh_sync_max_interpret_preview, 10), digits = 3,

Descriptives

Sample-level summary of the max-synchrony results above: how many couples show significant synchrony, how strong it tends to be, and how often mom versus partner leads.

code 
# Descriptive statistics across all couples
blpwh_sync_max_interpret_summary <- blpwh_sync_max_interpret %>%
  summarise(
    n_couples = n(),
    n_significant = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_significant = mean(significant, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    
    mean_max_sync = mean(max_abs_sync, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_max_sync = sd(max_abs_sync, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_lag = mean(max_lag, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_lag = sd(max_lag, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads
    n_mom_leads = sum(max_lag < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_partner_leads = sum(max_lag > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_concurrent = sum(max_lag == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    n_positive = sum(max_sync > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_negative = sum(max_sync < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

knitr::kable(blpwh_sync_max_interpret_summary, digits = 2,

Plot Max Synchrony

Three views of the max-synchrony distribution: how strong synchrony tends to be, where in time it tends to occur, and how strength and lag relate to each other.

code 
library(ggplot2)

# Distribution of maximum synchrony values
blpwh_hist_maxsync <- ggplot(blpwh_sync_max_interpret, aes(x = max_abs_sync, fill = significant)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#BBBBBB", "TRUE" = "#CC3311"), name = "Significant") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Maximum Synchrony Across Couples",
       x = "Maximum Absolute Correlation",
       y = "Number of Couples",
       fill = "Significant",
       caption = str_wrap("Histogram of each couple's maximum absolute time-lagged cross-correlation (positive interaction), colored by statistical significance.", width = 100)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 16), axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
code

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, alpha = 0.7) +

Grid Panel

A closer look at a handful of individual couples’ full cross-correlation functions, rather than the summarized max-synchrony view above.

code 
# Show multiple couples in a grid
blpwh_sync_ccfplot <- function(blpwh_sync_results, n_couples = 12) {
  # Select first n couples
  selected_ids <- unique(blpwh_sync_results$ID)[1:min(n_couples, length(unique(blpwh_sync_results$ID)))]

  blpwh_sync_results %>%
    filter(ID %in% selected_ids) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", size = 0.3) +
    geom_line(color = "#CC6677", size = 0.5) +
    geom_point(aes(color = significant), size = 1) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci),
                alpha = 0.15, fill = "#CC6677") +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#BBBBBB", "TRUE" = "#CC3311"), name = "Significant") +
    facet_wrap(~ ID, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
    labs(title = "Cross-Correlation Functions Across Couples",
         x = "Lag (seconds)",
         y = "Cross-Correlation",
         color = "Significant",
         caption = str_wrap("Full cross-correlation function by lag for a sample of couples, with 95% confidence bands and significant lags highlighted.", width = 100)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
          axis.title = element_text(size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
          panel.grid = element_blank())
}

# Make grid
blpwh_sync_ccfplot_p <- blpwh_sync_ccfplot(blpwh_sync_results, n_couples = 3)

Calculate Average

This collapses the couple-level CCFs into one sample-level average profile, showing the typical correlation at each lag across all couples along with the share of couples significant at that lag.

code 
# Compute mean CCF profile across all couples
blpwh_sync_avgccf <- blpwh_sync_results %>%
  group_by(lag) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_acf = mean(acf, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_acf = sd(acf, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    lower_se = mean_acf - 1.96 * se_acf,
    upper_se = mean_acf + 1.96 * se_acf,
    pct_significant = mean(significant, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .groups = "drop")

Plot Average

The x-axis label below follows the same direction as everywhere else in this file: negative lags (left) are mom leading, positive lags (right) are partner leading.

code 
# Plot average CCF
blpwh_sync_avgccf_plot <- ggplot(blpwh_sync_avgccf, aes(x = lag, y = mean_acf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_se, ymax = upper_se),
              alpha = 0.3, fill = "#CC6677") +
  geom_line(color = "#CC6677", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(size = pct_significant), color = "#CC6677") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 4), name = "% Couples\nSignificant") +
  labs(title = "Average Cross-Correlation Function Across All Couples",
       subtitle = "Shaded area represents 95% confidence interval",
       x = "Lag (seconds)\n\u2190 Mom leads | Partner leads \u2192",
       y = "Mean Cross-Correlation",
       caption = str_wrap("Mean cross-correlation function across all couples, with point size showing the percentage of couples significant at that lag.", width = 100)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 16), axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
        panel.grid = element_blank())

Time-Lagged

This restricts to non-zero lags and, separately, looks at how quickly synchrony first emerges for each couple.

code 
# Extract time-lagged (lag != 0)
blpwh_sync_lagged <- blpwh_sync_results %>% filter(lag != 0)

#max synchrony across non-zero lags
blpwh_sync_lagmax <- blpwh_sync_lagged %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  # Find the row with maximum absolute correlation for each couple
  slice_max(abs(acf), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  select(ID, 
         max_lag = lag,           # Lag at which max occurs
         max_sync = acf,          # Correlation value (with sign)
         max_abs_sync = acf,      # Will convert to absolute
         lower_ci, 
         upper_ci, 
         significant) %>%
  mutate(max_abs_sync = abs(max_sync)) %>%  # Add absolute value column
  ungroup()

##uses first sig lag
blpwh_sync_timetolag <- blpwh_sync_results %>%

  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(

    } else {

    .groups = "drop"
  )

Strongest Time-Lag

Among each couple’s significant lags only, this pulls the strongest one. The lag value has to be subset by significant before indexing with which.max(), since which.max() here returns a position within the significant-only subset, not within the full lag vector; indexing the full lag vector with that position (as the original code did) would pick the wrong lag whenever a couple has any non-significant lags before their strongest significant one. The strongest_acf line was already doing this correctly (subsetting acf before indexing), so strongest_lag is brought in line with it below.

code 
#uses strongest sig lag
blpwh_sync_summary <- blpwh_sync_results %>%
  mutate(significant = as.vector(significant)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    # Basic counts
    n_significant_lags = sum(significant),
    has_any_significant = any(significant),
    
    # If significant, what's the strongest? (lag subset by significant before indexing, to match acf below)
    strongest_lag = if(any(significant)) {
      lag[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    strongest_acf = if(any(significant)) {
      acf[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    # Specific patterns. Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads.
    has_concurrent = any(significant & lag == 0),
    has_mom_leads = any(significant & lag < 0),
    has_partner_leads = any(significant & lag > 0),
    
    .groups = "drop")

Summary Table - IDs

code 
library(gt)
library(dplyr)

# Create the formatted table
blpwh_sync_summarytable <- blpwh_sync_summary %>%
  # Select and order columns for display
  select(ID, n_significant_lags, strongest_lag, strongest_acf,
         has_concurrent, has_mom_leads, has_partner_leads) %>%
  # Take first 20 couples for display (or use head(10) for fewer)
  head(20) %>%

Compare Approaches

This lines up three different ways of summarizing a couple’s synchrony side by side: the time to the first significant lag, a simple mom-led/partner-led flag, and the single strongest significant lag. mom_led and partner_led replace the original parent_led/infant_led columns, which used parent-infant terminology left over from a different study’s template; this is a couple study, so the labels and the directions below both follow the mom/partner, negative-lag/positive-lag convention used throughout the rest of this file. The strongest_lag calculation has the same subset-before-index fix described above.

code 
# Compare the three approaches side-by-side for a few couples
blpwh_sync_compare <- blpwh_sync_results %>%
  mutate(significant = as.vector(significant)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    # Approach 1: First significant lag
    first_sig_lag = if(any(significant)) abs(lag[which(significant)[1]]) else NA_real_,
    
    # Approach 2: Categorical. Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads.
    mom_led = any(significant & lag < 0),
    partner_led = any(significant & lag > 0),
    
    # Approach 3: Strongest (lag subset by significant before indexing, to match acf)
    strongest_lag = if(any(significant)) lag[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))] else NA_real_,
    strongest_r = if(any(significant)) acf[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))] else NA_real_,
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Three Synchrony Approaches",
    subtitle = "First 10 couples"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(first_sig_lag, strongest_lag), decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = strongest_r, decimals = 3) %>%
  cols_label(
    ID = "Couple",
    first_sig_lag = "First Sig Lag",
    mom_led = "Mom Led",
    partner_led = "Partner Led",
    strongest_lag = "Strongest Lag",
    strongest_r = "Strongest r"
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Approach 1: First",
    columns = first_sig_lag
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Approach 2: Categorical",
    columns = c(mom_led, partner_led)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Approach 3: Strongest",

Negative Interaction

This section repeats the same synchrony calculation for negative warmth. The logic, the direction convention (negative lag, mom leads; positive lag, partner leads), and the corrected strongest_lag indexing are identical to the positive section above, so the narrative below stays brief.

Synchrony Calculation

code 
# Function to compute time-lagged cross-correlation synchrony between dyad members
compute_blnwh_sync <- function(df, lag = 20, n_boot = 1000) {
  
  # Remove rows with missing data for both mom and partner variables
  df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(blmnwh), !is.na(blfnwh))
  
  # Check if there's enough data to compute lagged correlations
  if (nrow(df) < lag + 1) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 1: Pre-whitening via ARIMA to remove autocorrelation ---
  # Fit ARIMA models to each person's time series to account for their individual temporal patterns
  fit_mom <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blmnwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  fit_partner <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blfnwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  
  # If either model fails, return NA results
  if (is.null(fit_mom) || is.null(fit_partner)) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # Extract residuals (pre-whitened series) - these represent deviations from each person's own temporal pattern
  res_mom <- residuals(fit_mom)
  res_partner <- residuals(fit_partner)
  
  # Combine residuals and remove any remaining missing values
  residuals_df <- tibble(res_mom, res_partner) %>% drop_na()
  if (nrow(residuals_df) < lag + 1) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 2: Compute observed cross-correlation function (CCF) ---
  # ccf(mom, partner)[k] estimates cor(mom[t+k], partner[t]).
  # Negative lags: mom leads partner. Positive lags: partner leads mom. Same convention as the positive section above.
  ccf_result <- ccf(residuals_df$res_mom, residuals_df$res_partner, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)
  observed_acf <- ccf_result$acf  # Cross-correlation values at each lag
  lags <- ccf_result$lag           # Lag values (e.g., -20 to +20)
  
  # --- STEP 3: Bootstrap to establish confidence intervals ---
  # Create matrix to store bootstrap results
  boot_corrs <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = length(lags))
  n <- nrow(residuals_df)
  
  # Generate null distribution by randomly shuffling residuals (breaks temporal coupling)
  for (i in 1:n_boot) {
    x_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_mom, n, replace = TRUE)      # Resample mom's residuals
    y_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_partner, n, replace = TRUE)  # Resample partner's residuals
    boot_ccf <- ccf(x_boot, y_boot, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)   # Compute CCF on shuffled data
    boot_corrs[i, ] <- boot_ccf$acf  # Store correlation values
  }
  
  # Calculate 95% confidence intervals from bootstrap distribution
  lower_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
  upper_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Determine significance: observed correlation falls outside 95% CI
  significant <- (observed_acf < lower_ci) | (observed_acf > upper_ci)
  
  # Return tibble with lag values, correlations, CIs, and significance
  tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(lags),
    acf = as.numeric(observed_acf),
    lower_ci = lower_ci,
    upper_ci = upper_ci,
    significant = significant
  )
}
code 
# Nest data by couple ID (creates list-column with each dyad's time series)
blnwh_sync_id <- BL_WH_Long %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  nest()

# Apply the synchrony function to each couple's data
blnwh_sync_id <- blnwh_sync_id %>%
  mutate(blnwh_sync_ccf = map(data, compute_blnwh_sync))

# Unnest results to get one row per couple per lag value

Max Synchrony

code 
# Extract max synchrony for each couple
blnwh_sync_max <- blnwh_sync_results %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  # Find the row with maximum absolute correlation for each couple
  slice_max(abs(acf), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  select(ID, 
         max_lag = lag,           # Lag at which max occurs
         max_sync = acf,          # Correlation value (with sign)
         max_abs_sync = acf,      # Will convert to absolute
         lower_ci, 
         upper_ci, 
         significant) %>%
  mutate(max_abs_sync = abs(max_sync)) %>%  # Add absolute value column
  ungroup()

Max Synchrony Interpretation

leaderN gives the same leader label as a numeric code (1 = mom, 2 = partner, 3 = concurrent), for downstream models that need a numeric rather than a character grouping variable.

code 
# Add interpretation columns
blnwh_sync_max_interpret <- blnwh_sync_max %>%
  mutate(
    # Who leads? Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads (see Positive Interaction section)
    leader = case_when(
      max_lag < 0 ~ "Mom leads",
      max_lag > 0 ~ "Partner leads",
      max_lag == 0 ~ "Concurrent",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    #leader numerical
    leaderN = case_when(
      max_lag < 0 ~ "1" , #mom
      max_lag > 0 ~ "2" , #partner
      max_lag == 0 ~ "3", #concurrent
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    # How much lead time?
    lead_time_seconds = abs(max_lag),
    # Direction of relationship
    relationship = case_when(
      max_sync > 0 ~ "Positive (same direction)",
      max_sync < 0 ~ "Negative (opposite direction)",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    # Strength categorization (example thresholds)
    strength = case_when(
      max_abs_sync >= 0.5 ~ "Strong",
      max_abs_sync >= 0.3 ~ "Moderate",
      max_abs_sync >= 0.1 ~ "Weak",
      TRUE ~ "Very weak"
    )
  )

# View interpreted results
blnwh_sync_max_interpret_preview <- blnwh_sync_max_interpret %>%
  select(ID, max_sync, max_lag, leader, lead_time_seconds,
         relationship, strength, significant)

# Show multiple couples in a grid
blnwh_sync_ccfplot <- function(blnwh_sync_results, n_couples = 12) {
  # Select first n couples
  selected_ids <- unique(blnwh_sync_results$ID)[1:min(n_couples, length(unique(blnwh_sync_results$ID)))]

  blnwh_sync_results %>%
    filter(ID %in% selected_ids) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", size = 0.3) +
    geom_line(color = "#CC6677", size = 0.5) +
    geom_point(aes(color = significant), size = 1) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci),
                alpha = 0.15, fill = "#CC6677") +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#BBBBBB", "TRUE" = "#CC3311"), name = "Significant") +
    facet_wrap(~ ID, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
    labs(title = "Cross-Correlation Functions Across Couples",
         x = "Lag (seconds)",
         y = "Cross-Correlation",
         color = "Significant",
         caption = str_wrap("Full cross-correlation function by lag for a sample of couples, with 95% confidence bands and significant lags highlighted.", width = 100)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
          axis.title = element_text(size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
          panel.grid = element_blank())
}

Heatmap Across Couples

Couples are identified only by their row order, not their real ID, and the y-axis is left unlabeled, so no participant identifiers appear on the public site.

code 
# Heatmap showing all couples' CCF profiles.
blnwh_sync_heatmap <- function(blnwh_sync_results, n_couples = 50) {
  selected_ids <- unique(blnwh_sync_results$ID)[1:min(n_couples, length(unique(blnwh_sync_results$ID)))]

  blnwh_sync_results %>%
    filter(ID %in% selected_ids) %>%
    mutate(couple_row = factor(match(ID, selected_ids))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = lag, y = couple_row, fill = acf)) +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#88CCEE", mid = "white", high = "#CC6677",
                         midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1),
                         name = "Correlation") +
    labs(title = "Cross-Correlation Heatmap: Random Assortment of Couples in the Study",
         x = "Lag (seconds)",
         y = NULL,
         caption = str_wrap("Correlation at every lag for a random assortment of couples in the study; couples are not individually identified. Red indicates positive correlation, blue negative, centered at zero.", width = 100)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
          axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12),
          panel.grid = element_blank())
}

Summary Table - ID

Same subset-before-index correction to strongest_lag as the positive section.

code 
#uses strongest sig lag
blnwh_sync_summary <- blnwh_sync_results %>%
  mutate(significant = as.vector(significant)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    # Basic counts
    n_significant_lags = sum(significant),
    has_any_significant = any(significant),
    
    # If significant, what's the strongest? (lag subset by significant before indexing, to match acf below)
    strongest_lag = if(any(significant)) {
      lag[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    strongest_acf = if(any(significant)) {
      acf[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    # Specific patterns. Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads.
    has_concurrent = any(significant & lag == 0),
    has_mom_leads = any(significant & lag < 0),
    has_partner_leads = any(significant & lag > 0),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )

---
title: Baseline Synchrony Calculation
toc-depth: 3
warning: false
editor: 
  markdown: 
    wrap: 72
---

# Purpose

This file runs the actual synchrony analysis that the 
[Baseline Synchrony Processing](Baseline-Synchrony_Processing.qmd) pipeline 
works up to. It takes the long-format positive- and negative-valence 
baseline warmth data produced by that pipeline and asks, second by second, 
whether mom's and partner's warmth track each other during the interaction, 
and whether one partner's warmth tends to change before the other's.

For each couple and each valence (positive, negative), the file fits an ARIMA 
model to each partner's warmth time series and uses the residuals (the 
pre-whitened series) to compute a time-lagged cross-correlation function (CCF) 
between mom and partner. A bootstrap null distribution, built by independently 
reshuffling each partner's residuals, establishes which lags show correlation 
stronger than chance. From that CCF, the file extracts several couple-level 
synchrony summaries: the single strongest lag overall, the strongest lag 
restricted to non-zero (time-lagged) lags, concurrent (lag-zero) synchrony, and 
how long it takes each couple to reach their first significant lag.

Throughout, a positive lag means partner's warmth at the current second 
correlates with mom's warmth a few seconds later, so partner is leading and mom
is following. A negative lag means the reverse: mom's warmth precedes partner's,
so mom is leading. This direction follows directly from how R's `ccf()` function
is called below (`ccf(mom, partner)`), and it is applied consistently to every 
leader/lag interpretation in this file.

The positive and negative sections mirror each other almost exactly, so the 
narrative under the negative section is kept brief where the logic has already 
been explained above.


**Load Packages**
```{r}
#| label: packages
#| warning: false
#| output: false

library(here)
library(nlme)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2) 
library(lavaan)
library(semTools)
library(jtools)
library(haven)
library(modsem)
library(forecast)
library(gt)
library(purrr)
```


Long-format positive- and negative-valence baseline warmth data, produced by the
[Baseline Synchrony Processing](Baseline-Synchrony_Processing.qmd) pipeline, are
read in from where that processed data already lives.

```{r}
#| label: load data
#| include: false

BL_WH_Long <- read_csv("C:/Users/rcm5550/OneDrive - The Pennsylvania State University/SFF Synchrony/Processed Data/BL_WH_Long.csv")
BL_WH_Pos_Long <- read_csv("C:/Users/rcm5550/OneDrive - The Pennsylvania State University/SFF Synchrony/Processed Data/BL_WH_Pos_Long.csv")
BL_WH_Neg_Long <- read_csv("C:/Users/rcm5550/OneDrive - The Pennsylvania State University/SFF Synchrony/Processed Data/BL_WH_Neg_Long.csv")

```

# Positive Interaction

This section calculates synchrony for positive warmth: how closely mom's and 
partner's warm, affectionate behavior track each other, and which partner's 
warmth tends to lead the other's during positive moments of the interaction.

## Synchrony Calculation

The function below does the full per-couple synchrony calculation in three steps.
First, it pre-whitens each partner's warmth series with `auto.arima()` so the 
cross-correlation reflects genuine coupling between partners rather than each 
person's own autocorrelation over time. Second, it computes the observed 
cross-correlation function between mom's and partner's residuals across a range
of lags. Third, it builds a bootstrap null distribution by independently 
reshuffling each partner's residuals, then flags any lag where the observed
correlation falls outside the resulting 95% interval as significant.

`ccf(mom, partner)` at lag *k* estimates the correlation between mom's residual 
at time *t + k* and partner's residual at time *t*. A positive *k* means mom's 
future value resembles partner's current value, so partner is leading. A 
negative *k* means mom's earlier value resembles partner's current value, so mom
is leading. 

```{r}
#| label: blpwh-sync-function

# Function to compute time-lagged cross-correlation synchrony between dyad members
compute_blpwh_sync <- function(df, lag = 20, n_boot = 1000) {
  
  # Remove rows with missing data for both mom and partner variables
  df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(blmpwh), !is.na(blfpwh))
  
  # Check if there's enough data to compute lagged correlations
  if (nrow(df) < lag + 1) return(
    tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 1: Pre-whitening via ARIMA to remove autocorrelation ---
  # Fit models to each person's time series to account for individual patterns
  fit_mom <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blmpwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  fit_partner <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blfpwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  
  # If either model fails, return NA results
  if (is.null(fit_mom) || is.null(fit_partner)) return(
    tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # Extract residuals (pre-whitened series) - these represent deviations from                                                     each person's own temporal pattern
  res_mom <- residuals(fit_mom)
  res_partner <- residuals(fit_partner)
  
  # Combine residuals and remove any remaining missing values
  residuals_df <- tibble(res_mom, res_partner) %>% drop_na()
  if (nrow(residuals_df) < lag + 1) return(
    tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 2: Compute observed cross-correlation function (CCF) ---
  # ccf(mom, partner)[k] estimates cor(mom[t+k], partner[t]).
  # Negative lags: 
  ### mom's earlier value resembles partner's current value -> mom leads partner.
  # Positive lags: 
  ### mom's future value resembles partner's current value -> partner leads mom.
  ccf_result <- ccf(
    residuals_df$res_mom, residuals_df$res_partner, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)
  observed_acf <- ccf_result$acf  # Cross-correlation values at each lag
  lags <- ccf_result$lag           # Lag values (e.g., -20 to +20)
  
  # --- STEP 3: Bootstrap to establish confidence intervals ---
  # Create matrix to store bootstrap results
  boot_corrs <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = length(lags))
  n <- nrow(residuals_df)
  
  # Generate null distribution by randomly shuffling residuals 
  ### breaks temporal coupling
  for (i in 1:n_boot) {
    # Resample mom's residuals
    x_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_mom, n, replace = TRUE)    
    # Resample partner's residuals
    y_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_partner, n, replace = TRUE)  
    # Compute CCF on shuffled data
    boot_ccf <- ccf(x_boot, y_boot, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)   
    # Store correlation values
    boot_corrs[i, ] <- boot_ccf$acf 
  }
  
  # Calculate 95% confidence intervals from bootstrap distribution
  lower_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
  upper_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Determine significance: observed correlation falls outside 95% CI
  significant <- (observed_acf < lower_ci) | (observed_acf > upper_ci)
  
  # Return tibble with lag values, correlations, CIs, and significance
  tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(lags),
    acf = as.numeric(observed_acf),
    lower_ci = lower_ci,
    upper_ci = upper_ci,
    significant = significant
  )
}
```

The function above runs once per couple. The chunk below nests the long-format
data by couple ID, applies the function to each couple's data in turn, and 
unnests the results back into one row per couple per lag.

```{r}
#| label: blpwh-sync-apply

# Nest data by couple ID (creates list-column with each dyad's time series)
blpwh_sync_id <- BL_WH_Long %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  nest()

# Apply the synchrony function to each couple's data
blpwh_sync_id <- blpwh_sync_id %>%
  mutate(blpwh_sync_ccf = map(data, compute_blpwh_sync))

# Unnest results to get one row per couple per lag value
blpwh_sync_results <- unnest(blpwh_sync_id, blpwh_sync_ccf)

blpwh_sync_results$lag <- as.numeric(blpwh_sync_results$lag)
```

## Max Synchrony

For each couple, this pulls out the single lag with the strongest absolute 
correlation across the full range of lags (including lag zero), regardless of
direction. This is the point of tightest overall coupling between mom's and 
partner's positive warmth.

```{r}
#| label: blpwh-max-sync

# Extract max synchrony for each couple
blpwh_sync_max <- blpwh_sync_results %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  # Find the row with maximum absolute correlation for each couple
  slice_max(abs(acf), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  select(ID, 
         max_lag = lag,           # Lag at which max occurs
         max_sync = acf,          # Correlation value (with sign)
         max_abs_sync = acf,      # Will convert to absolute
         lower_ci, 
         upper_ci, 
         significant) %>%
  mutate(max_abs_sync = abs(max_sync)) %>%  # Add absolute value column
  ungroup()

knitr::kable(head(blpwh_sync_max, 10), digits = 3,
             caption = 
               "Maximum Synchrony, Positive Interaction (first 10 couples)")
```

### Max Synchrony Interpretation

This translates the raw max-synchrony lag into a plain-language leader label, 
using the direction established above (negative lag, mom leads; positive lag, 
partner leads), and adds a rough strength category based on the size of the 
correlation.

```{r}
#| label: blpwh-max-sync-interpret

# Add interpretation columns
blpwh_sync_max_interpret <- blpwh_sync_max %>%
  mutate(
    # Who leads? Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads
    leader = case_when(
      max_lag < 0 ~ "Mom leads",
      max_lag > 0 ~ "Partner leads",
      max_lag == 0 ~ "Concurrent",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    # How much lead time?
    lead_time_seconds = abs(max_lag),
    # Direction of relationship
    relationship = case_when(
      max_sync > 0 ~ "Positive (same direction)",
      max_sync < 0 ~ "Negative (opposite direction)",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    # Strength categorization (example thresholds)
    strength = case_when(
      max_abs_sync >= 0.5 ~ "Strong",
      max_abs_sync >= 0.3 ~ "Moderate",
      max_abs_sync >= 0.1 ~ "Weak",
      TRUE ~ "Very weak"
    )
  )

blpwh_sync_max_interpret_preview <- blpwh_sync_max_interpret %>%
  select(ID, max_sync, max_lag, leader, lead_time_seconds,
         relationship, strength, significant)

knitr::kable(head(blpwh_sync_max_interpret_preview, 10), digits = 3, 
             caption = 
               "Interpreted Maximum Synchrony, Positive Interaction (first 10 couples)")
```

## Descriptives

Sample-level summary of the max-synchrony results above: how many couples show
significant synchrony, how strong it tends to be, and how often mom versus
partner leads.

```{r}
#| label: blpwh-descriptives

# Descriptive statistics across all couples
blpwh_sync_max_interpret_summary <- blpwh_sync_max_interpret %>%
  summarise(
    n_couples = n(),
    n_significant = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_significant = mean(significant, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    
    mean_max_sync = mean(max_abs_sync, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_max_sync = sd(max_abs_sync, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    mean_lag = mean(max_lag, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_lag = sd(max_lag, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads
    n_mom_leads = sum(max_lag < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_partner_leads = sum(max_lag > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_concurrent = sum(max_lag == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    n_positive = sum(max_sync > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_negative = sum(max_sync < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

knitr::kable(blpwh_sync_max_interpret_summary, digits = 2,
             caption = 
               "Descriptive Summary of Maximum Synchrony, Positive Interaction")
```

## Calculate Average

This collapses the couple-level CCFs into one sample-level average profile, showing the typical correlation at each lag across all couples along with the share of couples significant at that lag.

```{r}
#| label: calc-blpwh-avgccf

# Compute mean CCF profile across all couples
blpwh_sync_avgccf <- blpwh_sync_results %>%
  group_by(lag) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_acf = mean(acf, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_acf = sd(acf, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    lower_se = mean_acf - 1.96 * se_acf,
    upper_se = mean_acf + 1.96 * se_acf,
    pct_significant = mean(significant, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .groups = "drop")
```

### Plot Average

The x-axis label below follows the same direction as everywhere else in this file: negative lags (left) are mom leading, positive lags (right) are partner leading.

```{r}
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_se, ymax = upper_se),
              alpha = 0.3, fill = "#CC6677") +
  geom_line(color = "#CC6677", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(size = pct_significant), color = "#CC6677") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 4), name = "% Couples\nSignificant") +
  labs(title = "Average Cross-Correlation Function Across All Couples",
       subtitle = "Shaded area represents 95% confidence interval",
       x = "Lag (seconds)\n\u2190 Mom leads | Partner leads \u2192",
       y = "Mean Cross-Correlation",
       caption = str_wrap("Mean cross-correlation function across all couples, with point size showing the percentage of couples significant at that lag.", width = 100)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 16), axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
```

```{r}
  filter(lag == 0) %>%

         concurrent_lower = lower_ci, concurrent_upper = upper_ci)
```

## Time-Lagged

This restricts to non-zero lags and, separately, looks at how quickly synchrony first emerges for each couple.

```{r}
#| label: blpwh-lagmax

# Extract time-lagged (lag != 0)
blpwh_sync_lagged <- blpwh_sync_results %>% filter(lag != 0)

#max synchrony across non-zero lags
blpwh_sync_lagmax <- blpwh_sync_lagged %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  # Find the row with maximum absolute correlation for each couple
  slice_max(abs(acf), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  select(ID, 
         max_lag = lag,           # Lag at which max occurs
         max_sync = acf,          # Correlation value (with sign)
         max_abs_sync = acf,      # Will convert to absolute
         lower_ci, 
         upper_ci, 
         significant) %>%
  mutate(max_abs_sync = abs(max_sync)) %>%  # Add absolute value column
  ungroup()

# View results
knitr::kable(head(blpwh_sync_lagmax, 10), digits = 3, caption = str_wrap("Maximum Time-Lagged Synchrony, Positive Interaction (first 10 couples)", width = 100))
```

```{r}
#| label: pos time lag to synchrony

##uses first sig lag
blpwh_sync_timetolag <- blpwh_sync_results %>%
  mutate(significant = as.vector(significant)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    has_significant = any(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    time_lag_to_sync = if (any(significant, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      abs(lag[which(significant)[1]])
    } else {
      NA_integer_
    },
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(head(blpwh_sync_timetolag, 10), caption = str_wrap("Time to First Significant Synchrony, Positive Interaction (first 10 couples)", width = 100))
```

### Strongest Time-Lag

Among each couple's significant lags only, this pulls the strongest one. The lag value has to be subset by `significant` before indexing with `which.max()`, since `which.max()` here returns a position within the significant-only subset, not within the full lag vector; indexing the full `lag` vector with that position (as the original code did) would pick the wrong lag whenever a couple has any non-significant lags before their strongest significant one. The `strongest_acf` line was already doing this correctly (subsetting `acf` before indexing), so `strongest_lag` is brought in line with it below.

```{r}
#| label: blpwh-summary

#uses strongest sig lag
blpwh_sync_summary <- blpwh_sync_results %>%
  mutate(significant = as.vector(significant)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    # Basic counts
    n_significant_lags = sum(significant),
    has_any_significant = any(significant),
    
    # If significant, what's the strongest? (lag subset by significant before indexing, to match acf below)
    strongest_lag = if(any(significant)) {
      lag[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    strongest_acf = if(any(significant)) {
      acf[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    # Specific patterns. Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads.
    has_concurrent = any(significant & lag == 0),
    has_mom_leads = any(significant & lag < 0),
    has_partner_leads = any(significant & lag > 0),
    
    .groups = "drop")
```

## Summary Table - IDs

```{r}
#| label: blpwh-summarytable
library(gt)
library(dplyr)

# Create the formatted table
blpwh_sync_summarytable <- blpwh_sync_summary %>%
  # Select and order columns for display
  select(ID, n_significant_lags, strongest_lag, strongest_acf,
         has_concurrent, has_mom_leads, has_partner_leads) %>%
  # Take first 20 couples for display (or use head(10) for fewer)
  head(20) %>%
  
  # Create gt table
  gt() %>%
  
  # Add title and subtitle
  tab_header(
    title = "Dyadic Synchrony Analysis",
    subtitle = "Cross-Correlation Results by Couple"
  ) %>%
  
  # Format numeric columns
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(strongest_acf),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(strongest_lag),
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  
  # Rename columns with readable labels
  cols_label(
    ID = "Couple ID",
    n_significant_lags = "# Significant Lags",
    strongest_lag = "Strongest Lag (sec)",
    strongest_acf = "Correlation (r)",
    has_concurrent = "Concurrent Sync",
    has_mom_leads = "Mom Leads",
    has_partner_leads = "Partner Leads"
  ) %>%
  
  # Color code the boolean columns
  data_color(
    columns = c(has_concurrent, has_mom_leads, has_partner_leads),
    colors = scales::col_factor(
      palette = c("lightgray", "lightgreen"),
      domain = c(FALSE, TRUE)
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Color code correlation strength
  data_color(
    columns = strongest_acf,
    colors = scales::col_numeric(
      palette = c("white", "#CC6677", "#332288"),
      domain = c(0, max(blpwh_sync_summary$strongest_acf, na.rm = TRUE))
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Color code lag direction
  data_color(
    columns = strongest_lag,
    colors = scales::col_numeric(
      palette = c("#88CCEE", "white", "#CC6677"),
      domain = c(
        min(blpwh_sync_summary$strongest_lag, na.rm = TRUE),
        max(blpwh_sync_summary$strongest_lag, na.rm = TRUE)
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Bold the column headers
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
      cell_fill(color = "#CC6677")
    ),
    locations = cells_column_labels(everything())
  ) %>%
  
  # Style the title
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold", size = "large"),
    locations = cells_title(groups = "title")
  ) %>%
  
  # Add alternating row colors
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#F5F5F5"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = seq(2, 20, 2))
  ) %>%
  
  # Add footnotes
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Significant lags determined by bootstrap confidence intervals (\u03b1 = .05)",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = n_significant_lags)
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Negative lag = Mom leads; Positive lag = Partner leads; Zero = Concurrent",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = strongest_lag)
  ) %>%
  
  # Add source note
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Analysis based on pre-whitened ARIMA residuals with 1000 bootstrap iterations"
  ) %>%
  
  # Table size
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(14),
    column_labels.font.size = px(14),
    heading.title.font.size = px(16),
    heading.subtitle.font.size = px(13)
  ) %>%

  # Adjust column widths
  cols_width(
    ID ~ px(90),
    n_significant_lags ~ px(130),
    strongest_lag ~ px(140),
    strongest_acf ~ px(120),
    has_concurrent ~ px(120),
    has_mom_leads ~ px(120),
    has_partner_leads ~ px(140)
  )

# Display the table
blpwh_sync_summarytable
```

```{r}
        TRUE ~ x
      )
    }

      cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
```

## Compare Approaches

This lines up three different ways of summarizing a couple's synchrony side by side: the time to the first significant lag, a simple mom-led/partner-led flag, and the single strongest significant lag. `mom_led` and `partner_led` replace the original `parent_led`/`infant_led` columns, which used parent-infant terminology left over from a different study's template; this is a couple study, so the labels and the directions below both follow the mom/partner, negative-lag/positive-lag convention used throughout the rest of this file. The `strongest_lag` calculation has the same subset-before-index fix described above.

```{r}
#| label: blpwh-compare
# Compare the three approaches side-by-side for a few couples
blpwh_sync_compare <- blpwh_sync_results %>%
  mutate(significant = as.vector(significant)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    # Approach 1: First significant lag
    first_sig_lag = if(any(significant)) abs(lag[which(significant)[1]]) else NA_real_,
    
    # Approach 2: Categorical. Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads.
    mom_led = any(significant & lag < 0),
    partner_led = any(significant & lag > 0),
    
    # Approach 3: Strongest (lag subset by significant before indexing, to match acf)
    strongest_lag = if(any(significant)) lag[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))] else NA_real_,
    strongest_r = if(any(significant)) acf[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))] else NA_real_,
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Three Synchrony Approaches",
    subtitle = "First 10 couples"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(first_sig_lag, strongest_lag), decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = strongest_r, decimals = 3) %>%
  cols_label(
    ID = "Couple",
    first_sig_lag = "First Sig Lag",
    mom_led = "Mom Led",
    partner_led = "Partner Led",
    strongest_lag = "Strongest Lag",
    strongest_r = "Strongest r"
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Approach 1: First",
    columns = first_sig_lag
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Approach 2: Categorical",
    columns = c(mom_led, partner_led)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Approach 3: Strongest",
    columns = c(strongest_lag, strongest_r)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
                 cell_fill(color = "#CC6677")),
    locations = cells_column_labels(everything())
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
                 cell_fill(color = "#332288")),
    locations = cells_column_spanners(spanners = everything())
  )

blpwh_sync_compare
```

# Negative Interaction

This section repeats the same synchrony calculation for negative warmth. The logic, the direction convention (negative lag, mom leads; positive lag, partner leads), and the corrected `strongest_lag` indexing are identical to the positive section above, so the narrative below stays brief.

## Synchrony Calculation

```{r}
#| label: blnwh-sync-function
# Function to compute time-lagged cross-correlation synchrony between dyad members
compute_blnwh_sync <- function(df, lag = 20, n_boot = 1000) {
  
  # Remove rows with missing data for both mom and partner variables
  df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(blmnwh), !is.na(blfnwh))
  
  # Check if there's enough data to compute lagged correlations
  if (nrow(df) < lag + 1) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 1: Pre-whitening via ARIMA to remove autocorrelation ---
  # Fit ARIMA models to each person's time series to account for their individual temporal patterns
  fit_mom <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blmnwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  fit_partner <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blfnwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  
  # If either model fails, return NA results
  if (is.null(fit_mom) || is.null(fit_partner)) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # Extract residuals (pre-whitened series) - these represent deviations from each person's own temporal pattern
  res_mom <- residuals(fit_mom)
  res_partner <- residuals(fit_partner)
  
  # Combine residuals and remove any remaining missing values
  residuals_df <- tibble(res_mom, res_partner) %>% drop_na()
  if (nrow(residuals_df) < lag + 1) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 2: Compute observed cross-correlation function (CCF) ---
  # ccf(mom, partner)[k] estimates cor(mom[t+k], partner[t]).
  # Negative lags: mom leads partner. Positive lags: partner leads mom. Same convention as the positive section above.
  ccf_result <- ccf(residuals_df$res_mom, residuals_df$res_partner, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)
  observed_acf <- ccf_result$acf  # Cross-correlation values at each lag
  lags <- ccf_result$lag           # Lag values (e.g., -20 to +20)
  
  # --- STEP 3: Bootstrap to establish confidence intervals ---
  # Create matrix to store bootstrap results
  boot_corrs <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = length(lags))
  n <- nrow(residuals_df)
  
  # Generate null distribution by randomly shuffling residuals (breaks temporal coupling)
  for (i in 1:n_boot) {
    x_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_mom, n, replace = TRUE)      # Resample mom's residuals
    y_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_partner, n, replace = TRUE)  # Resample partner's residuals
    boot_ccf <- ccf(x_boot, y_boot, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)   # Compute CCF on shuffled data
    boot_corrs[i, ] <- boot_ccf$acf  # Store correlation values
  }
  
  # Calculate 95% confidence intervals from bootstrap distribution
  lower_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
  upper_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Determine significance: observed correlation falls outside 95% CI
  significant <- (observed_acf < lower_ci) | (observed_acf > upper_ci)
  
  # Return tibble with lag values, correlations, CIs, and significance
  tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(lags),
    acf = as.numeric(observed_acf),
    lower_ci = lower_ci,
    upper_ci = upper_ci,
    significant = significant
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: blnwh-sync-apply
# Nest data by couple ID (creates list-column with each dyad's time series)
blnwh_sync_id <- BL_WH_Long %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  nest()

# Apply the synchrony function to each couple's data
blnwh_sync_id <- blnwh_sync_id %>%
  mutate(blnwh_sync_ccf = map(data, compute_blnwh_sync))

# Unnest results to get one row per couple per lag value
blnwh_sync_results <- unnest(blnwh_sync_id, blnwh_sync_ccf)

blnwh_sync_results$lag <- as.numeric(blnwh_sync_results$lag)
```

## Max Synchrony

```{r}
#| label: blnwh-max-sync
# Extract max synchrony for each couple
blnwh_sync_max <- blnwh_sync_results %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  # Find the row with maximum absolute correlation for each couple
  slice_max(abs(acf), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  select(ID, 
         max_lag = lag,           # Lag at which max occurs
         max_sync = acf,          # Correlation value (with sign)
         max_abs_sync = acf,      # Will convert to absolute
         lower_ci, 
         upper_ci, 
         significant) %>%
  mutate(max_abs_sync = abs(max_sync)) %>%  # Add absolute value column
  ungroup()

knitr::kable(head(blnwh_sync_max, 10), digits = 3, caption = str_wrap("Maximum Synchrony, Negative Interaction (first 10 couples)", width = 100))
```

### Max Synchrony Interpretation

`leaderN` gives the same leader label as a numeric code (1 = mom, 2 = partner, 3 = concurrent), for downstream models that need a numeric rather than a character grouping variable.

```{r}
#| label: blnwh-max-sync-interpret
# Add interpretation columns
blnwh_sync_max_interpret <- blnwh_sync_max %>%
  mutate(
    # Who leads? Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads (see Positive Interaction section)
    leader = case_when(
      max_lag < 0 ~ "Mom leads",
      max_lag > 0 ~ "Partner leads",
      max_lag == 0 ~ "Concurrent",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    #leader numerical
    leaderN = case_when(
      max_lag < 0 ~ "1" , #mom
      max_lag > 0 ~ "2" , #partner
      max_lag == 0 ~ "3", #concurrent
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    # How much lead time?
    lead_time_seconds = abs(max_lag),
    # Direction of relationship
    relationship = case_when(
      max_sync > 0 ~ "Positive (same direction)",
      max_sync < 0 ~ "Negative (opposite direction)",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    # Strength categorization (example thresholds)
    strength = case_when(
      max_abs_sync >= 0.5 ~ "Strong",
      max_abs_sync >= 0.3 ~ "Moderate",
      max_abs_sync >= 0.1 ~ "Weak",
      TRUE ~ "Very weak"
    )
  )

# View interpreted results
blnwh_sync_max_interpret_preview <- blnwh_sync_max_interpret %>%
  select(ID, max_sync, max_lag, leader, lead_time_seconds,
         relationship, strength, significant)

knitr::kable(head(blnwh_sync_max_interpret_preview, 10), digits = 3, caption = str_wrap("Interpreted Maximum Synchrony, Negative Interaction (first 10 couples)", width = 100))
```

## Calculate Average

```{r}
#| label: calc-blnwh-avgccf
# Compute mean CCF profile across all couples
blnwh_sync_avgccf <- blnwh_sync_results %>%
  group_by(lag) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_acf = mean(acf, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_acf = sd(acf, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    lower_se = mean_acf - 1.96 * se_acf,
    upper_se = mean_acf + 1.96 * se_acf,
    pct_significant = mean(significant, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## Summary Table - ID

Same subset-before-index correction to `strongest_lag` as the positive section.

```{r}
#| label: blnwh-summary
#uses strongest sig lag
blnwh_sync_summary <- blnwh_sync_results %>%
  mutate(significant = as.vector(significant)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    # Basic counts
    n_significant_lags = sum(significant),
    has_any_significant = any(significant),
    
    # If significant, what's the strongest? (lag subset by significant before indexing, to match acf below)
    strongest_lag = if(any(significant)) {
      lag[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    strongest_acf = if(any(significant)) {
      acf[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    # Specific patterns. Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads.
    has_concurrent = any(significant & lag == 0),
    has_mom_leads = any(significant & lag < 0),
    has_partner_leads = any(significant & lag > 0),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
  # Select and order columns for display
  select(ID, n_significant_lags, strongest_lag, strongest_acf,
         has_concurrent, has_mom_leads, has_partner_leads) %>%
  # Take first 20 couples for display (or use head(10) for fewer)

  # Create gt table
  gt() %>%

    title = "Dyadic Synchrony Analysis",

  # Format numeric columns
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(strongest_acf),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(strongest_lag),
    decimals = 0
  ) %>%
  
  # Rename columns with readable labels
  cols_label(
    ID = "Couple ID",
    n_significant_lags = "# Significant Lags",
    strongest_lag = "Strongest Lag (sec)",
    strongest_acf = "Correlation (r)",
    has_concurrent = "Concurrent Sync",
    has_mom_leads = "Mom Leads",
    has_partner_leads = "Partner Leads"
  ) %>%
  
  # Color code the boolean columns
  data_color(
    columns = c(has_concurrent, has_mom_leads, has_partner_leads),
    colors = scales::col_factor(
      palette = c("lightgray", "lightgreen"),
      domain = c(FALSE, TRUE)
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Color code correlation strength
  data_color(
    columns = strongest_acf,
    colors = scales::col_numeric(
      palette = c("white", "#CC6677", "#332288"),
      domain = c(0, max(blnwh_sync_summary$strongest_acf, na.rm = TRUE))
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Color code lag direction
  data_color(
    columns = strongest_lag,
    colors = scales::col_numeric(
      palette = c("#88CCEE", "white", "#CC6677"),
      domain = c(
        min(blnwh_sync_summary$strongest_lag, na.rm = TRUE),
        max(blnwh_sync_summary$strongest_lag, na.rm = TRUE)
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Bold the column headers
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
      cell_fill(color = "#CC6677")
    ),
    locations = cells_column_labels(everything())
  ) %>%
  
  # Style the title
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold", size = "large"),
    locations = cells_title(groups = "title")
  ) %>%
  
  # Add alternating row colors
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "#F5F5F5"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = seq(2, 20, 2))
  ) %>%
  
  # Add footnotes
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Significant lags determined by bootstrap confidence intervals (\u03b1 = .05)",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = n_significant_lags)
  ) %>%
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Negative lag = Mom leads; Positive lag = Partner leads; Zero = Concurrent",
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = strongest_lag)
  ) %>%
  
  # Add source note
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Analysis based on pre-whitened ARIMA residuals with 1000 bootstrap iterations"
  ) %>%
  
  # Table size
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(14),
    column_labels.font.size = px(14),
    heading.title.font.size = px(16),
    heading.subtitle.font.size = px(13)
  ) %>%

  # Adjust column widths
  cols_width(
    ID ~ px(90),
    n_significant_lags ~ px(130),
    strongest_lag ~ px(140),
    strongest_acf ~ px(120),
    has_concurrent ~ px(120),
    has_mom_leads ~ px(120),
    has_partner_leads ~ px(140)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: blnwh-summarystats
# Create a summary statistics table instead of individual couples
blnwh_sync_summarystats <- blnwh_sync_summary %>%
  summarise(
    n_couples = n(),
    
    # Synchrony prevalence
    pct_any_significant = mean(has_any_significant, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_concurrent = mean(has_concurrent, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_mom_leads = mean(has_mom_leads, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_partner_leads = mean(has_partner_leads, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    
    # Lag characteristics
    mean_n_sig_lags = mean(n_significant_lags, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_strongest_lag = median(strongest_lag, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Correlation strength
    mean_strongest_acf = mean(abs(strongest_acf), na.rm = TRUE),
    median_strongest_acf = median(abs(strongest_acf), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  
  # Reshape for better display
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) %>%
  
  # Create gt table
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Dyadic Synchrony: Summary Statistics",
    subtitle = paste0("N = ", nrow(blnwh_sync_summary), " couples")
  ) %>%
  
  # Format values
  fmt_number(
    columns = Value,
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  
  # Improve metric labels
  text_transform(
    locations = cells_body(columns = Metric),
    fn = function(x) {
      case_when(
        x == "n_couples" ~ "Total Couples",
        x == "pct_any_significant" ~ "% with Significant Synchrony",
        x == "pct_concurrent" ~ "% with Concurrent Synchrony",
        x == "pct_mom_leads" ~ "% with Mom Leading",
        x == "pct_partner_leads" ~ "% with Partner Leading",
        x == "mean_n_sig_lags" ~ "Mean # Significant Lags",
        x == "median_strongest_lag" ~ "Median Strongest Lag (sec)",
        x == "mean_strongest_acf" ~ "Mean Correlation Strength",
        x == "median_strongest_acf" ~ "Median Correlation Strength",
        TRUE ~ x
      )
    }
  ) %>%
  
  # Style
  tab_style(
    style = list(
      cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
      cell_fill(color = "#CC6677")
    ),
    locations = cells_column_labels(everything())
  ) %>%
  
  cols_label(
    Metric = "Statistic",
    Value = "Value"
  ) %>%
  
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Pre-whitened cross-correlation with bootstrap significance testing"
  )
```

## Compare Approaches

Same three-approach comparison as the positive section, with the same `mom_led`/`partner_led` and `strongest_lag` fixes. This section had no heading in the original file; it's added here so the table doesn't appear to float under "Summary Table - All" above it.

```{r}
#| label: blnwh-compare
# Compare the three approaches side-by-side for a few couples
blnwh_sync_compare <- blnwh_sync_results %>%
  mutate(significant = as.vector(significant)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    # Approach 1: First significant lag
    first_sig_lag = if(any(significant)) abs(lag[which(significant)[1]]) else NA_real_,
    
    # Approach 2: Categorical. Negative lag = mom leads, positive lag = partner leads.
    mom_led = any(significant & lag < 0),
    partner_led = any(significant & lag > 0),
    
    # Approach 3: Strongest (lag subset by significant before indexing, to match acf)
    strongest_lag = if(any(significant)) lag[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))] else NA_real_,
    strongest_r = if(any(significant)) acf[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))] else NA_real_,
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Three Synchrony Approaches",
    subtitle = "First 10 couples"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(first_sig_lag, strongest_lag), decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = strongest_r, decimals = 3) %>%
  cols_label(
    ID = "Couple",
    first_sig_lag = "First Sig Lag",
    mom_led = "Mom Led",
    partner_led = "Partner Led",
    strongest_lag = "Strongest Lag",
    strongest_r = "Strongest r"
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Approach 1: First",
    columns = first_sig_lag
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Approach 2: Categorical",
    columns = c(mom_led, partner_led)
  ) %>%
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Approach 3: Strongest",
    columns = c(strongest_lag, strongest_r)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
                 cell_fill(color = "#CC6677")),
    locations = cells_column_labels(everything())
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold", color = "white"),
                 cell_fill(color = "#332288")),
    locations = cells_column_spanners(spanners = everything())
  )

blnwh_sync_compare
```
